plain_title: Faking or causing illness without an obvious reason
also_known_as: factitious disorder imposed on another (Munchausen by proxy)
one_liner: Deliberately producing or faking illness in oneself, or in someone in one's care, without an obvious external reward.
in_simple_words: Factitious disorder is when a person deliberately fakes or causes illness or injury, in themselves (imposed on self) or in someone they care for, usually a child (imposed on another), without an outside motive like money. The driver is a deep need to be seen as ill or as a caregiver. It's rare and often rooted in trauma. Imposed on another is abuse and handled as child protection. Treatment is possible but hard, because the person often can't admit it.
what_it_can_feel_like: I don't fully know why I did it. The hospital was the only place I felt looked after.
Being confronted was devastating. Being offered therapy instead of just being discharged was what changed things.
As the child it was done to, I grew up believing I was sick. Learning the truth took years.
common_signs: Faking, exaggerating, or deliberately causing symptoms or injury
Presenting oneself (or another) as ill, impaired, or injured
No obvious external reward, like money or avoiding duties
Often many hospital admissions, unusual or inconsistent test results, or symptoms that worsen when unobserved
In 'imposed on another': a child with unexplained, recurring illness in one person's care

myths_vs_facts.myth: People with factitious disorder are just attention-seekers who should be ignored.
myths_vs_facts.fact: It's a serious mental health condition, usually rooted in trauma. Ignoring it leaves the person, and sometimes a child, at real risk.
Malingering is faking for an external gain, like money or avoiding work, and isn't a mental disorder. Factitious disorder has no such gain.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Somatic symptom disorder and FND are types of faking too.
myths_vs_facts.fact: No. In those conditions symptoms are genuinely experienced. Factitious disorder is the only one involving deliberate deception.

how_common.plain: Factitious disorder is thought to be rare, around 1 in 100 hospital patients in some estimates, though it's largely unrecognized and the true rate is unknown.
how_common.figure: Estimated around 1% of hospital inpatients in some studies; true prevalence unknown because of deception

what_helps.plain_summary: Treatment is challenging. The first step is a careful, non-punitive approach: a consistent clinician, limiting harmful tests and procedures, and offering psychological help without forcing a confession. Longer-term psychotherapy can address the underlying needs and trauma. Any co-occurring depression or personality difficulties are treated. When a child is involved, protecting the child comes first, through child protection services, with support for the whole family.
evidence_based_options: Psychotherapy for underlying trauma and needs
Child protection procedures and family support when imposed on another
self_help_that_supports_care: If you recognize yourself: telling one clinician the truth is the bravest and most effective step
Asking for therapy rather than another admission
For families and clinicians: concern for the child's safety overrides everything
Support for adults who were harmed as children by a caregiver's factitious behaviour

when_to_reach_out: If you've been faking or causing illness and want to stop, a GP or mental health professional can help you without judgement. If you're worried a child is being made ill by a caregiver, contact child protection services or a child abuse helpline now.
is_not: Genuinely experienced symptoms (somatic symptom disorder, FND) are not factitious. Faking for money, drugs, or to avoid duties is malingering, not a disorder. Illness anxiety involves real fear, not deception.
hope_note: People with factitious disorder can recover when they find a relationship safe enough to be honest in. Children affected by it can heal with the truth and support.

content_notes: Imposed on another is child abuse; child-protection links required.
